raw_case_text:
A 23-year-old Hispanic male presented to our care with a sore throat and odynophagia to liquid and solids for 3 days. He denied any fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or shortness of breath. He claimed that he had frequent respiratory and gastrointestinal infections when he was a child. On a previous hospital admission 2 years ago, he was discovered to have a lung abscesses (Staphylococcus aureus) and oral candidiasis. The computed tomography (CT) of the chest on the previous admission revealed a large consolidation involving the right lung and posterior segment of the left lower lobe with an air fluid level. These bilateral lung abscesses were drained and he was treated for aspiration pneumonia with clindamycin 300 mg PO four times a day for one month upon discharge. The CT of the chest (Figure 1) after drainage of the abscess revealed residual 6 cm thin walled cyst in the posterior aspect of the of left midlung field. Other past medical problems included recurrent Staphylococcus aureus skin infections. He had no family history of any immunodeficiency disorders. He admitted to smoking 1 pack of cigarettes per week for the last 9 years and social alcohol use. He denied any illicit drugs use.
Initial vital signs were significant for hypertension (blood pressure: 147/85), tachycardia (heart rate: 116), and tachypnea (respiratory rate: 25 breaths per minute). Physical examination revealed a cachectic individual with multiple eczematous lesions and folliculitis over his entire body. He had white lesions resembling thrush on his tongue, palate, and oropharynx. It was noted that he had retention of his primary teeth. Breath sounds were decreased bilaterally on auscultation. He was tachycardic but without murmurs. He had a decreased muscle mass of all four extremities. The initial lab work-up (Table 1) was only significant for acute renal insufficiency (BUN 25 mg/dL and creatinine 2.2. mg/dL), hypocalcemia (calcium 7.9 mmol/L), hypoalbuminemia (albumin 2.8 g/dL), and hypoproteinemia (7.9 mmol/L). The chest radiograph (Figure 2) on admission revealed a left lung cyst.
Our initial impression was oral/esophageal candidiasis and the possibility of an immunodeficiency disorder. For the treatment of oral/esophageal candidiasis, he was started on fluconazole 100 mg IV daily. The HIV test was negative. Other lab work-ups (Table 2) was ordered to rule out various immunodeficiency disorders. All the immunoglobulins (Ig) were within normal range except that IgE was very elevated (>5000 IU/mL). The normal value of IgE was <114 IU/mL. Genetic mutation analysis revealed a novel mutation affecting the transactivation domain of the STAT3 gene at exon 22. This provided a definite diagnosis of autosomal dominant hyper IgE syndrome which correlates with the clinical presentation. These results confirmed our suspicion of hyper IgE syndrome (Job's syndrome). No curative treatment is available for hyper IgE syndrome. We treated his multiple skin infections with mupirocin 2% ointment and started prophylactic treatment of recurrent skin and pulmonary infections with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160 mg tab every 12 hours to prevent recurrent staphylococcal infections.
Approximately one year after previous, he presented again with a productive cough with greenish sputum, fever, chills, generalized weakness, eczema, chest pain, and shortness of breath for 4 days. On the day of admission he had 3 bouts of hemoptysis. The CT of the chest (Figure 3) revealed the same cavitation measuring 5.6 cm in the superior segment of the left lower lobe (LLL) that contained soft tissue density that was suggestive of a mycetoma. A bronchoscopy was performed on this admission with findings of hemoptysis and cavitation in the LLL. The analysis of the bronchoalveloar lavage fluid did not reveal any pneumocystis or fundal organisms. He was discharged on amoxicillin-sulbactum 500 mg tab every 12 hours and itraconazole 200 mg tab every 12 hours. Even though the patient had recurrent infections typical of hyper IgE as a child, he never received an immunodeficiency investigation. Partly because hyper IgE is a rare disease that can have a variety of presentations and not all physicians may consider it in their differential diagnosis, another reason as stated by the patient was that he was treated for the infection and then either lost to follow up or went to another hospital once another infection recurred. This case demonstrates the chronic debilitating course of a patient with hyper IgE.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old Hispanic male with a history of recurrent childhood infections and bilateral Staphylococcus aureus lung abscesses presented initially with a 3-day history of sore throat and odynophagia, and re-presented 1 year later with a 4-day history of productive cough with greenish sputum, fever, chills, chest pain, dyspnea, and hemoptysis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with 3 days of sore throat and odynophagia to solids and liquids without fever or respiratory symptoms, leading to a clinical and genetic diagnosis of autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (Job's syndrome). Despite initiation of prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160 mg PO q12h), he re-presented 1 year later with a 4-day history of productive cough with greenish sputum, fever, chills, generalized weakness, worsening eczema, pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, and three episodes of frank hemoptysis on the day of readmission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Frequent childhood respiratory and gastrointestinal infections; bilateral Staphylococcus aureus lung abscesses ( drained 2 years prior and treated with 1 month of oral clindamycin 300 mg QID, leaving a residual 6 cm thin-walled cyst in the left mid-lung field) and oral candidiasis; recurrent S. aureus skin infections/folliculitis; retained primary dentition. Social history: Smoked 1 pack of cigarettes/week for 9 years, social alcohol use, no illicit drug use; negative family history of immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial admission positive for sore throat, odynophagia, oral thrush, and chronic eczematous/follicular skin lesions (negative for fever, chills, cough, dyspnea, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea); 1-year readmission positive for productive cough with green sputum, 3 bouts of hemoptysis, fever, chills, generalized weakness, chest pain, and shortness of breath.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission vital signs: Blood pressure 147/85 mmHg, heart rate 116 beats/min, respiratory rate 25 breaths/min. Physical findings: Cachectic male with generalized muscle wasting across all four extremities; diffuse eczematous skin lesions and folliculitis over the entire body; white thrush plaques on the tongue, palate, and oropharynx; retained primary teeth; bilaterally decreased breath sounds on lung auscultation; regular tachycardia without cardiac murmurs.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission laboratory tests: BUN 25 mg/dL, serum creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, calcium 7.9 mmol/L, serum albumin 2.8 g/dL, total protein 7.9 mmol/L; HIV test negative; normal serum IgG, IgA, and IgM levels. Initial admission chest radiograph: Residual 6 cm thin-walled cyst in the left mid-lung field.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological and genetic workup: Markedly elevated serum IgE >5,000 IU/mL (normal <114 IU/mL); STAT3 gene sequencing identified a novel heterozygous mutation in exon 22 affecting the transactivation domain, confirming autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (Job's syndrome). One-year readmission chest CT: Persistent 5.6 cm cavity in the superior segment of the left lower lobe (LLL) containing an intracavitary soft-tissue density suggestive of a mycetoma. Readmission bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Active hemoptysis and cavitation in the LLL; BAL fluid analysis was negative for Pneumocystis and fungal organisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (Job's syndrome; confirmed by serum IgE >5,000 IU/mL, retained primary teeth, recurrent S. aureus skin/lung abscesses, and a novel exon 22 STAT3 transactivation domain mutation) complicated by oral/esophageal candidiasis and subsequent recurrent superinfection/suspected intracavitary mycetoma within a chronic 5.6 cm left lower lobe pneumatocele/cavity (with Pneumocystis excluded on BAL). Plan and clinical course: Initial oral/esophageal candidiasis and skin infections were treated with IV fluconazole (100 mg daily), topical mupirocin 2% ointment, and prophylactic oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160 mg q12h). Upon readmission 1 year later with hemoptysis and left lower lobe cavitary superinfection/mycetoma, he was stabilized and discharged on oral amoxicillin-sulbactam (500 mg q12h) and oral itraconazole (200 mg q12h).
